notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Why TCP must deliver in order — RFC 9293 §3.4: Sequence Numbers

  • The transport built to remove it — RFC 9000 §2: Streams

  • HTTP/2's multiplexing, and what it can't fix — RFC 9113 §5: Streams and Multiplexing

  • Measured impact of moving to HTTP/3 — Comparing HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2 Performance

  • Bonus — the TCP-side treatment: High Performance Browser Networking: Head-of-Line Blocking

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one-sentence cause? TCP promises an ordered byte stream, so byte N+1 cannot be delivered before byte N.
How long is the stall? At least one RTT (fast retransmit), or up to the RTO if there aren't enough dup ACKs.
Did HTTP/2 fix it? It fixed the application-layer version. The transport-layer one got worse — one connection, all streams.
What does QUIC change? Per-stream loss recovery: a lost packet stalls only the stream whose bytes it carried.
Where does HOL blocking still exist in HTTP/3? Within a single stream, and in HPACK/QPACK header-table dependencies.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

TCP delivers a strictly ordered byte stream, so if segment 2 of 5 is lost, the receiver holds 3, 4 and 5 in its buffer and hands your application nothing until the retransmission of 2 arrives — at least one RTT later. That's fine for a single file. It's ruinous once you multiplex, because HTTP/2 puts a hundred independent streams on one connection, and one lost packet belonging to one image stalls every other stream behind it. The blocking isn't a bug in loss recovery; it's the ordering guarantee itself, which is why the fix required leaving TCP.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through what the receiver is actually doing during the stall.

🎯 Really testing: whether you locate the stall at the receiver's delivery boundary, or vaguely "in the network".

The data isn't lost from the receiver's perspective — it's sitting right there. Segments arriving after the gap are accepted into the receive buffer (assuming SACK, so the sender knows not to resend them) and tracked as an out-of-order block. What the receiver cannot do is hand them to the application, because recv() on a TCP socket contractually returns bytes in stream order, and the missing bytes come first. So the buffer fills with data the application would happily process and isn't allowed to see.

Meanwhile the receiver emits duplicate ACKs — repeating "I still want byte 1461" — which is the signal that triggers fast retransmit at the sender after three of them. If enough data is in flight to generate three dup ACKs, recovery takes about one RTT. If it isn't — a small response, or a loss near the end of a transfer — no dup ACKs arrive, nothing triggers fast retransmit, and the sender waits out the full retransmission timeout, which has a 1-second floor on Linux. That's the difference between a 50ms hiccup and a 1-second freeze, and it's why tail loss is disproportionately painful.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

HTTP/2 multiplexes 100 streams onto one connection. Is that better or worse than HTTP/1.1's six connections?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up whenever someone says "HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking".

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the fix moved the problem down a layer rather than removing it.

Better on a clean network, worse on a lossy one, and the crossover is around 2% loss. HTTP/1.1's six parallel connections were a workaround: six independent TCP streams meant a loss on one stalled a sixth of your traffic, and browsers capped at six because more connections meant more handshakes, more congestion-control instances competing, and more server state. HTTP/2 removes the cap, gives you real prioritisation, header compression and one warm congestion window instead of six cold ones — genuinely better, most of the time.

The cost is that you've concentrated everything onto a single failure domain. Under HTTP/1.1, one lost packet blocked one connection's worth of work; under HTTP/2, one lost packet blocks all streams, because they share one byte stream and one sequence space. On a good fixed-line connection with sub-0.1% loss this never surfaces. On a congested mobile network at 2%+ loss, HTTP/2 can measurably lose to HTTP/1.1 — which is exactly the observation that motivated QUIC. So the honest answer is that HTTP/2 traded many small blocking domains for one large one, and bet on loss being rare; QUIC is the correction for when that bet is wrong.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Your LLM token stream over SSE stutters for exactly some users. Where's the head-of-line blocking?

📍 Seen in the wild: the "streaming works locally, arrives in chunks in production" incident, which usually has three candidate causes and this is one.

At the transport, and it's amplified by everything above it. Token streaming produces small, frequent writes — 20-60 bytes every few tens of milliseconds — and small writes are the worst case for loss recovery, because there's rarely enough data in flight to generate three duplicate ACKs. So a single lost segment doesn't get fast-retransmitted; it waits for the RTO, floored at 1 second on Linux. The user sees tokens flowing smoothly and then a full second of nothing followed by a burst of ten tokens at once. What runs out here isn't a resource — it's the in-flight data needed to trigger the cheap recovery path.

It presents as a bimodal time-between-tokens distribution, and that's the diagnostic. Median inter-token latency looks perfect; p99 has a hard cluster right at ~1000ms, which is the RTO floor wearing a disguise. If you only chart mean or median tokens-per-second the incident is invisible. Chart the inter-token gap distribution and the 1-second spike is unmistakable. Confirm with ss -ti on the server socket — retrans climbing and rto:1000 on the affected connections — and check whether the same users are the ones on mobile networks. The mitigations are architectural rather than tuning: put an edge terminator close to the user so the lossy leg is short and the RTO is computed from a small RTT, and move to HTTP/3 where the stall is confined to one stream.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the delivery path for a streaming chat product, 100k concurrent users, token-by-token. Where does HOL blocking bite and what do you do?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can place this concept in a topology rather than describe it in the abstract.

The highest-stakes constraint is that time-to-first-token and inter-token smoothness are the product, and both are latency distributions rather than averages — so the design target is the tail, and head-of-line blocking is a tail phenomenon. That immediately says: shorten the lossy leg. Terminate the user's connection at an edge PoP, and carry the traffic from edge to inference origin over the provider's backbone where loss is negligible. The user's exposure to HOL blocking is now confined to the last mile, where you can't remove it but can make its RTT small — and RTO scales with RTT, so a 20ms edge RTT gives a far cheaper stall than a 200ms origin RTT.

The hops compose as: browser → anycast edge (HTTP/3 preferred, HTTP/2 fallback, TLS terminated) → pooled HTTP/2 connection over backbone → regional gateway → inference service, with SSE end to end. Two decisions carry the note's content. Offer HTTP/3, because per-stream recovery is exactly the property this workload needs and the win concentrates on the lossy mobile users who are otherwise your worst experiences — keep HTTP/2 as fallback since UDP is blocked often enough. And disable proxy buffering on the SSE path (proxy_buffering off / X-Accel-Buffering: no), because a buffering proxy produces the identical symptom — tokens arriving in bursts — for an entirely different reason, and you must rule it out before blaming the transport.

The failure I'd monitor first is the inter-token gap distribution at p99, segmented by network type and HTTP version. Aggregate streaming latency will look healthy while a mobile-heavy cohort sees second-long freezes. Segmenting by HTTP version also gives you the direct measurement of whether HTTP/3 is earning its complexity on your actual traffic — which is the number to bring to the discussion rather than a claim from a vendor blog.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Stack Multiplexing Loss of one packet stalls… Where HOL blocking remains
HTTP/1.1, one connection None — one request at a time That request, and everything queued behind it Application layer: strict request ordering
HTTP/1.1, six connections Six parallel byte streams One sixth of in-flight work Both layers, but blast radius is 1/6
HTTP/1.1 pipelining Requests in flight, responses ordered Every response behind the slow one Application layer — why it was abandoned
HTTP/2 over TCP Many streams, one connection Every stream on the connection Transport layer only, but connection-wide
HTTP/3 over QUIC Many streams, per-stream recovery Only the stream that lost the packet Within one stream; QPACK header dependencies
Separate TCP connections per stream Full isolation Only that stream None — but you pay N handshakes and N cold windows

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

The tunnel is single-file, and the stalled car is at the front.

📖 Story

Cars enter a single-file tunnel numbered in order and must exit in that order. Car 2 breaks down; 3, 4 and 5 arrive fine and park behind it, engines running. Nothing exits until a replacement for car 2 is driven in — even though the waiting cars were never damaged and their passengers are going somewhere else entirely.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • Numbered cars exiting in order = TCP's ordered byte-stream delivery contract

  • Car 2 breaking down = the lost segment

  • Cars 3–5 parked with engines running = the receive buffer holding out-of-order data the application can't see

  • Passengers going somewhere else = independent HTTP/2 streams, blocked by a loss that has nothing to do with them

  • Driving in a replacement = the retransmission, one RTT away at best

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The diagram is the whole mechanism. Stream 1 and stream 5 had no packet loss at all and were still stalled, because at the TCP layer there are no streams — only one sequence space. HTTP/2's frame headers, which are what carry the stream IDs, live inside the byte stream that TCP is refusing to deliver. TCP cannot honour a distinction it cannot see.

The stall duration has two very different regimes, and knowing which one you're in is the practical payoff:

Fast retransmit path — three duplicate ACKs trigger retransmission without waiting for a timer. Stall ≈ 1 RTT. Requires enough data in flight after the gap to generate three dup ACKs.

RTO path — not enough subsequent data, so no dup ACKs. Stall = the retransmission timeout, computed as RTO = SRTT + 4 × RTTVAR (RFC 6298) but floored at 1 second on Linux. On a 20ms path that floor is 50× the RTT.

That floor is why small, frequent writes — token streams, chat messages, telemetry heartbeats — suffer far more than bulk transfer. Bulk transfer always has data in flight and almost always takes the cheap path; a token stream frequently has nothing behind the lost segment and takes the expensive one.

Why QUIC fixes it, in one sentence: QUIC carries stream IDs in the packet rather than in the byte stream, so the transport itself knows which stream a lost packet belonged to, and can deliver every other stream while recovering that one. That is the entire architectural difference — everything else about QUIC follows from needing a transport that can see stream boundaries.

Where the blocking lives at each layer

  HTTP/1.1 pipelining   ┌─ application layer ─┐  responses must be ordered
  HTTP/2 over TCP       ┌─ transport layer ───┐  one byte stream, all streams share it
  HTTP/3 over QUIC      ┌─ per-stream ────────┐  blocking confined to the losing stream

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is p99 latency and its shape, not p50. Head-of-line blocking never moves the median — most packets aren't lost — so a service can look perfectly healthy on average while a meaningful slice of users experiences second-long freezes. The signature is a bimodal or spiked tail: a cluster of measurements sitting at the RTO floor. Teams that chart only averages will not see this until users report it.

It also matters because it determines whether HTTP/3 is worth the operational cost for you. The honest framing is that HTTP/3's benefit is concentrated entirely in your lossy-network cohort — mobile, congested Wi-Fi, long international paths. If your traffic is desktop clients on fixed lines, HTTP/2 is fine and HTTP/3 buys little; if a third of your users are on mobile networks in high-latency regions, it's one of the larger tail-latency wins available. Segmenting p99 by network type is what turns that from opinion into a decision.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# 1. Is this connection actually retransmitting? The direct evidence.
#    retrans:X/Y = current/total. rto: is the timeout in ms — 1000 means the floor.
ss -ti state established '( dport = :443 )' | grep -E 'rtt|retrans|rto|cwnd'

# 2. System-wide retransmission rate. Compare over an interval, not once.
nstat -az TcpRetransSegs TcpExtTCPLostRetransmit TcpExtTCPTimeouts

# 3. Reproduce it deliberately — 2% loss on egress, the HTTP/2 crossover point.
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 2% delay 50ms
#    ...run your streaming client, watch inter-token gaps...
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

# 4. Rule out the impostor first: a buffering proxy produces the same symptom.
curl -N -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://api.example.com/v1/stream
#    -N disables curl's own buffering; http_version tells you 2 or 3.

# The impostor, and its fix. A buffering proxy batches SSE chunks and looks
# exactly like transport-layer blocking from the client's side.
location /v1/stream {
    proxy_pass http://inference_upstream;
    proxy_buffering off;          # emit each chunk as it arrives, don't accumulate
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;      # a long stream is not an idle connection
    proxy_set_header Connection '';  # allow upstream keepalive on HTTP/1.1
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

An SSE token stream from api.example.com, client on a mobile network, 50ms RTT, ~2% loss, run under the netem conditions above:

📥 t=0ms       SSE stream open, tokens arriving
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [1] tokens 1-14 delivered      gaps: 38-45ms each — healthy
    │
    ▼
❌ [2] segment carrying token 15 lost in the network        t=612ms
    │
    ▼
⚠️ [3] tokens 16, 17 arrive, buffered, NOT delivered        t=650, 690ms
    │       receiver holds them — gap in the sequence space
    │       only 2 segments behind the gap → 2 dup ACKs → no fast retransmit
    ▼
⏱️ [4] sender waits out the RTO                              rto:1000 (floor)
    │
    ▼
🔄 [5] retransmit of token 15's segment                      t=1612ms
    │
    ▼
✅ [6] tokens 15, 16, 17 all delivered at once               t=1662ms
        inter-token gap for token 15: 1050ms
        tokens 16 and 17: 0ms apart — the burst

[1] Steady state looks perfect: ~40ms between tokens, which is the model's generation rate rather than anything network-related. Any dashboard averaging over this window reports a healthy stream.

[2] One segment lost. Nothing observable happens yet on either side — the sender doesn't know, and the receiver doesn't know a segment is missing until a later one arrives.

[3] This is the critical step and the reason token streams are the pathological case. Only two more tokens are generated before the timeout, so only two duplicate ACKs are sent. Fast retransmit needs three. The cheap recovery path is unavailable, not because of the network but because of the traffic shape.

[4] The sender falls back to the retransmission timer. RFC 6298 computes RTO from smoothed RTT, which on a 50ms path would be ~250ms — but Linux floors RTO at 1 second, and the floor wins. This single line is where the outage lives.

[5] The retransmission goes out at t=1612ms, a full second after the loss, and arrives 50ms later.

[6] Three tokens land simultaneously. The user sees a one-second freeze followed by a stutter. Median inter-token latency across the whole stream is still ~40ms; p99 is 1050ms, sitting exactly on the RTO floor — the fingerprint to look for.

10. When TO Use This

Head-of-line blocking is a property to design against rather than to use, so this section is about when accepting it is correct:

  • Accept it when loss is genuinely rare and multiplexing pays. Inside a data centre or over a provider backbone, loss is well under 0.1%; HTTP/2's single warm connection beats six cold ones and you will never observe the stall.

  • Accept it when ordering is a requirement anyway. A database wire protocol or a transactional stream needs in-order delivery, so the blocking is the guarantee you're paying for, not a defect.

  • Accept it rather than sharding across many connections. Splitting streams over N connections removes the blocking but costs N handshakes, N cold congestion windows and N congestion-control instances competing with each other — usually a worse trade than the stall you avoided.

  • Design around it when the workload is small, frequent writes over a lossy last mile. Token streams, live updates, chat. That's the RTO-floor case from Section 9, and it's where edge termination and HTTP/3 earn their keep.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't put a high-multiplexing HTTP/2 connection across a lossy long path and expect it to behave. Degradation isn't gradual: below ~1% loss you see nothing, above ~2% the tail falls apart as every stream shares every stall. The symptom is a p99 cliff with a healthy p50, which reads like a server problem and isn't.

  • Don't reach for HTTP/3 before ruling out the buffering proxy. A proxy accumulating SSE chunks produces a visually identical symptom — smooth output becoming bursty — for a completely different reason, and it's far more common. proxy_buffering off costs nothing to check; migrating to HTTP/3 is a platform project. Check the cheap thing first.

  • Don't shard across parallel connections as your fix. It's the HTTP/1.1 workaround in new clothing: you get isolation and pay for it with handshakes, cold windows, and multiple congestion controllers fighting over the same bottleneck. Below about four connections it's sometimes worth it; beyond that you're usually making the tail worse.

  • Don't tune tcp_rto_min to escape the floor. It's tempting after reading Section 9 and it's the wrong instinct: lowering the RTO floor causes spurious retransmissions on any path whose RTT estimate is briefly wrong, which adds load precisely when the network is already struggling. Shorten the path instead.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking."

✅ Reality: It fixed the application-layer version — HTTP/1.1's rule that responses return in request order. The transport-layer version got structurally worse, because collapsing six connections into one means a single lost packet now stalls every stream instead of a sixth of them. Saying "HTTP/2 fixed HOL blocking" without that qualification is the single most common wrong statement about the protocol.

❌ Misconception: "The stall lasts one RTT."

✅ Reality: Only on the fast-retransmit path, which needs three duplicate ACKs and therefore enough data in flight behind the gap. Small frequent writes often don't have it, and then you wait out the RTO — floored at 1 second on Linux regardless of how fast the path is. The 1-second version is the one that generates incidents.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed QUIC's advantage was that UDP is lighter, and that dropping TCP's overhead was the point. It isn't — QUIC re-implements reliability, ordering and congestion control, so it isn't lighter at all. The point is where the stream IDs live: QUIC puts them in the packet so the transport can see stream boundaries, while HTTP/2 puts them inside the byte stream TCP is refusing to deliver. Once I had that, every other QUIC design decision followed.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Saying "HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking" flat. It's the trap this topic exists to catch. Always name which layer, and volunteer that the transport-layer version got worse — that single qualification is what the question is testing for.

Describing it as a loss-recovery inefficiency. It isn't a performance defect to be tuned away; it's a direct consequence of the ordered-delivery API contract. Framing it as inefficiency leads to answers about tuning, when the real answers are architectural — shorten the path, or change transport.

Quoting HTTP/3 benchmarks without conditions. HTTP/3's advantage is concentrated in lossy conditions. Someone will ask "and on a clean fixed line?", where the answer is roughly no difference. Bring the condition with the claim.

Ignoring the middle. In practice, "my stream is bursty" is a buffering proxy far more often than it's transport blocking. An answer that jumps straight to QUIC without mentioning proxy_buffering describes a two-endpoint world that production doesn't have.

Confident numbers with no source. "HTTP/3 is 30% faster" invites an immediate challenge. "The gain concentrates above roughly 2% loss, and I'd measure our own p99 segmented by network type before committing" is the defensible version.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Fast-retransmit trigger 3 duplicate ACKs Below this, recovery falls back to the RTO timer RFC 5681 §3.2
Stall on fast retransmit ~1 RTT The cheap path; needs data in flight behind the gap RFC 5681 §3.2
RTO formula SRTT + 4 × RTTVAR Computed from measured RTT RFC 6298 §2
Linux minimum RTO 1 second TCP_RTO_MIN; the floor that dominates on fast paths RFC 6298 §2.4 recommends 1s
HTTP/1.1 browser connection cap 6 per origin The pre-HTTP/2 workaround, and its blast radius RFC 9113 background
Loss rate where HTTP/2 degrades ~2% and above Where one shared connection loses to six independent ones Cloudflare HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2
QUIC stream isolation Per-stream loss recovery Stream IDs carried in the packet, not the byte stream RFC 9000 §2

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Multiplexing removes queueing delay on a clean path and concentrates stall risk on a lossy one; the trade is median versus tail
💰 Cost One connection is cheaper in server state than six; the saving is real and is what you give back when you shard for isolation
🔒 Security / visibility QUIC encrypts most of its transport header, so the loss and retransmission behaviour you can read from tcpdump on TCP is opaque on QUIC
📈 Scale Blast radius scales with multiplexing depth: 100 streams on one connection means one packet can stall 100 units of work
🔧 Ops complexity HTTP/3 means UDP through your LBs and firewalls, a fallback path, and a second protocol to debug — real cost against a tail-only benefit
🐛 Debuggability The symptom is indistinguishable from a buffering proxy, a slow upstream, or client-side rendering. Distinguishing them needs ss -ti retransmit counters, not guesses

16. Real World Usage

QUIC exists because of this problem specifically. Google's measurements on lossy mobile networks showed SPDY/HTTP/2's multiplexing being undermined by transport-layer blocking, and concluded that fixing TCP was impossible on any useful timescale because TCP lives in kernels and middleboxes. Building a new transport on UDP was the cheaper path — a decision that is really about deployment velocity as much as protocol design.

The gRPC-on-HTTP/2 case makes it concrete for backend engineers. Many RPCs multiplex onto one long-lived connection, so one lost packet delays every in-flight call between those two services. On an intra-DC path that's invisible; across regions or over a VPN it turns into correlated latency spikes across unrelated calls, which is a genuinely confusing thing to debug because the affected requests have nothing in common except the connection.

LLM token streaming is the current high-profile case, and it's the one worth having an opinion on: small frequent writes over consumer networks is the exact traffic shape that lands on the RTO path rather than the fast-retransmit path, which is why streaming products care about HTTP/3 more than page-load products ever did.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym. Two that appear throughout: RTO — Retransmission Timeout, the timer that fires when duplicate ACKs never arrive, floored at 1 second on Linux. SACK — Selective Acknowledgement, which lets the receiver report exactly which blocks arrived so the sender resends only the gap. SACK makes recovery efficient but does nothing about the blocking, because the constraint is delivery order, not retransmission volume.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 19-tcp-vs-udp.md — the ordering guarantee that causes this, and why UDP doesn't have it

  • TCP sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission — the recovery mechanism whose two paths set the stall duration

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • HTTP/2 binary framing and multiplexing (Section 6) — where streams are defined and why TCP can't see them

  • HTTP/3 and QUIC (Section 6) — the transport built to remove this

  • SSE token streaming end to end (Section 16) — the production case where this is most visible

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Sharding across parallel connections — full isolation at the cost of N handshakes and N cold windows; the HTTP/1.1 approach

  • Edge termination — doesn't remove the blocking, shortens the leg it happens on, which shrinks both the RTT and the RTO

  • UDP with application-level recovery — correct for media, wrong for anything where ordering matters; see the WebRTC path

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Buffering proxies — produce an identical symptom for a different reason; always ruled out first

  • Connection pooling — decides multiplexing depth, and therefore the blast radius of a single loss

  • Congestion control — determines how much data is in flight, which decides whether recovery takes the 1-RTT path or the 1-second one

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

The usual framing is a debugging scenario rather than a design one: "your streaming responses arrive smoothly in staging and in bursts for some production users — walk me through it." What's being tested is whether you can enumerate the candidate causes in cost order (buffering proxy, then transport blocking, then client rendering), pick the diagnostic that separates them, and only then propose a fix. The design version follows immediately: "now design the delivery path so this doesn't happen", which is where edge termination and protocol choice become the answer.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10k concurrent streams Nothing transport-related; a single region handles it. Blocking affects only the mobile cohort Ship HTTP/2, disable proxy buffering, measure the tail before doing more
100k concurrent streams Long-haul RTT dominates the RTO for distant users, so every stall is expensive Edge PoPs to shorten the lossy leg; pooled backhaul over the backbone
1M concurrent streams Multiplexing depth per connection makes each loss stall many streams; UDP blocked for a slice of users HTTP/3 with enforced HTTP/2 fallback; cap streams per connection; regional inference to remove the long leg entirely

The cost dimension is that edge PoPs and HTTP/3 both add spend — egress through more points of presence, and a second protocol path to operate. Both are justified by tail latency for a segment of users, so the business case has to be made on that segment's size, not on an aggregate average that will show almost no change.

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x: p99 inter-token gap develops a cluster at the RTO floor while p50 stays flat. Invisible on any average-based dashboard.

  • At 100x: correlated stalls across unrelated streams sharing a connection, so latency spikes look like a backend problem and aren't.

  • Operationally: the HTTP/3 fallback path silently carries most traffic because a firewall blocks UDP, and nobody notices because both paths "work" — the tail-latency win you paid for was never delivered.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Inter-token gap distribution at p99, segmented by network type and HTTP version. Alert on a cluster near 1000ms, not on the mean. This is the single metric that makes the whole topic observable.

  • TCP retransmission rate per connection (ss -ti, TcpRetransSegs) on the terminating tier — the direct evidence separating transport blocking from a buffering proxy.

  • Share of traffic on HTTP/3 versus the HTTP/2 fallback. If HTTP/3 was adopted for tail latency, this ratio is the measurement of whether you actually got it.

notes.title: Nagle's Algorithm & TCP_NODELAY
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The original algorithm — RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks (Nagle, 1984)

  • TCP_NODELAY and the delayed-ACK interaction — Linux tcp(7)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does Nagle's algorithm do? Withholds a small write while any earlier data is still unacknowledged.
Where does the ~40ms delay come from? Nagle interacting with the receiver's delayed ACK timer — not Nagle alone.
The fix, and its cost? TCP_NODELAY disables Nagle. Cost: more small packets on the wire.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Nagle's algorithm stops TCP flooding the network with tiny packets: if there's unacknowledged data outstanding, a new small write is buffered until an ACK arrives or a full segment's worth accumulates. It pairs badly with delayed ACK, where the receiver waits up to ~40ms before acknowledging in case it can piggyback on a reply. Sender waits for an ACK, receiver waits for data — a standoff broken only by the delayed-ACK timer. That's the classic 40ms mystery latency, and it shows up in write-write-read protocols. TCP_NODELAY disables Nagle and is set by default in most RPC stacks for exactly this reason; the cost is more small packets, which on modern links is a trade almost everyone should take.

notes.title: Keepalives, Idle Timeouts & Half-Open Connections

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
Why doesn't TCP notice the peer is gone?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Your connection pool intermittently throws resets on the first request after quiet periods. Diagnose and fix.
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • TCP keepalive requirements and defaults — RFC 9293 §3.8.4: TCP Keep-Alives

  • Linux keepalive tunables — Linux tcp(7): tcp_keepalive_time, _intvl, _probes

  • Half-open connections — RFC 9293 §3.5.1: Half-Open Connections and Other Anomalies

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Linux default keepalive idle time? 7200 seconds — two hours. Useless for any real pool; you must lower it.
What is a half-open connection? One side thinks it's ESTABLISHED; the peer is gone. TCP is silent until you write.
The rule for pool idle timeout? Strictly below the shortest timeout in the path — LB, NAT, or peer.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An idle TCP connection sends nothing, so neither side learns when the other disappears — a crashed peer, a NAT mapping expiring, a load balancer reaping at 60 seconds. The socket stays ESTABLISHED locally and fails only on the next write, which is why connection pools serve dead sockets and applications see intermittent resets that look like flakiness. TCP keepalive exists to detect this, but Linux's default idle time is two hours, so it's effectively off unless you set it. The practical rule is that your pool's idle timeout must be shorter than the shortest timeout anywhere in the path.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why doesn't TCP notice the peer is gone?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that TCP connection state is an illusion maintained by two independent machines.

Because there's nothing to notice. A TCP connection isn't a circuit; it's two endpoints each holding a data structure that says "we're connected". If the peer's machine loses power, no FIN and no RST is ever sent — there's nobody left to send one. Your kernel's state is unchanged, the socket reads as ESTABLISHED, and select/epoll will happily report it writable. This is the half-open connection of RFC 9293 §3.5.1, and it's indistinguishable from a healthy idle connection by inspection alone.

Detection only happens when you send something. You write, get no ACK, retransmit on a backing-off schedule for several minutes, and eventually the connection fails with ETIMEDOUT. If the peer did reboot and receives your segment for a connection it doesn't know about, it replies RST and you fail fast with ECONNRESET — which is why the symptom is usually a reset on the first request after an idle period. TCP keepalive is the mechanism for probing before that happens, but its defaults are so long (7200s idle, then 9 probes 75s apart) that it's useless as shipped. Either lower the three sysctls per-socket, or implement heartbeats at the application layer — which is what every long-lived protocol ends up doing, because an application-level ping also proves the application is alive, not merely the kernel.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Your connection pool intermittently throws resets on the first request after quiet periods. Diagnose and fix.

📍 Seen in the wild: the most common connection-pool bug there is, usually reported as "the upstream is flaky" and blamed on the wrong team.

🎯 Really testing: whether you find the shortest timeout in the path rather than tuning your own end in isolation.

The pattern is diagnostic on its own: failures cluster after idle periods, hit only the first request on a reused connection, and disappear entirely under sustained load. That's a socket the far end closed while your pool kept it. The usual culprit is a load balancer's idle timeout — 60 seconds by default on an AWS ALB — which closes the connection toward your client; if that FIN is missed or the connection was silently dropped rather than closed, your pool hands out a dead socket and the first write returns ECONNRESET.

The fix has three parts and the order matters. First, set your pool's idle timeout below the shortest timeout in the path — every LB, proxy, NAT gateway and the peer's own server timeout; if the ALB is 60s, use 45s or lower, and don't guess, enumerate the hops. Second, enable retry-on-idempotent so a reset on a reused connection is retried once on a fresh one — HTTP clients call this idempotent-request retry, and it turns a user-visible error into a millisecond of extra latency. Third, enable TCP keepalive on pooled sockets with sane values (30–60s idle rather than 7200) so mappings stay alive and death is detected early. The trap worth naming is NAT: gateways can drop UDP mappings in 30 seconds and idle TCP mappings in minutes, silently and without an RST, so a connection through NAT can die without either endpoint being told — which is exactly the half-open case from Tier 1.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Timeout Typical default What it does Why it bites
Linux tcp_keepalive_time 7200s (2 hours) Idle before the first probe So long it's effectively off; must be lowered per-socket
Linux tcp_keepalive_intvl / _probes 75s / 9 Probe spacing and count ~11 further minutes before the connection is declared dead
AWS ALB idle timeout 60s Closes idle client and target connections The number that silently kills pooled and streaming connections
nginx keepalive_timeout 75s Idle upstream keep-alive Must exceed your client's pool timeout, or the same race appears
NAT gateway UDP mapping as low as 30s Drops the mapping, no notification Why every UDP protocol sends its own keepalive

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism has no clever part — that's what makes it a reliable source of production incidents. There is no signal on an idle TCP connection, so a peer that vanishes leaves your endpoint's state untouched. TCP keepalive addresses this by sending a probe segment with a sequence number one below the next expected byte, which forces the peer to respond with an ACK without delivering anything to its application. Linux gates it on three sysctls, and the shipped defaults add up badly:

Time to detect a dead peer with Linux defaults: tcp_keepalive_time (7200s) + tcp_keepalive_probes (9) × tcp_keepalive_intvl (75s) = 7200 + 675 ≈ 2 hours 11 minutes. For a connection pool that's indistinguishable from no detection at all. Set them per-socket via SO_KEEPALIVE and TCP_KEEPIDLE, not globally.

The rule that falls out of the diagram is a strict inequality: your idle timeout < every timeout in the path. Enumerate the hops — client pool, any proxy, the load balancer, any NAT gateway, the server's own keep-alive setting — and set yours below the minimum. The failure is always the same shape: whoever times out first closes, and whoever notices last serves a dead socket.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't rely on TCP keepalive as a health check. It proves a kernel is answering, not that your application is functional. A process deadlocked on a lock or a thread pool answers keepalives perfectly while serving nothing. Application-level heartbeats are what you actually want; keepalive is for reaping dead sockets and holding NAT mappings.

  • Don't set aggressive keepalives on a server with very many connections. At 100k connections a 15-second interval is over 6,000 probe packets per second of pure overhead, plus wakeups. Keepalive intervals belong on the client side of a pool, where connection counts are small.

  • Don't set your pool idle timeout equal to the load balancer's. Equal is a race, and races produce exactly the intermittent, unreproducible resets that consume days. Leave a clear margin — an ALB at 60s wants a pool at 45s or less.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "TCP keepalive is enabled by default, so dead connections get cleaned up."

✅ Reality: SO_KEEPALIVE is off by default per socket, and even when enabled Linux waits two hours before the first probe. Almost every language's HTTP client leaves it off. If you haven't explicitly configured it, you have no keepalive.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed a socket reading as ESTABLISHED meant the peer was reachable. It only means this kernel still holds that state. The peer may have rebooted, the NAT mapping may be gone, and nothing will tell you until you write. "Established" is a local belief, not a verified fact — and once I internalised that, most connection-pool weirdness stopped being surprising.

notes.title: Sockets, Ports & the Ephemeral Port Range

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
"A server can only handle 65,535 connections because there are only 65,535 ports." What's wrong with that?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
An API gateway proxying to one backend service starts throwing EADDRNOTAVAIL. What's happening and what do you change?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Port registry and the dynamic range — RFC 6335 §6: Port Number Ranges

  • Ephemeral port selection — RFC 6056: Recommendations for Transport-Protocol Port Randomization

  • Linux socket and port tunables — Linux ip(7): ip_local_port_range

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What makes a connection unique? The 4-tuple: src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port. Not the port alone.
How many outbound connections to one upstream IP:port? ~28,232 on default Linux — the ephemeral range 32768–60999.
First error you hit, and what it means? EMFILE (out of file descriptors, ulimit -n) before anything network-shaped.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A connection is identified by a four-tuple — source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port — so a server listening on one port can hold millions of connections, because each client contributes a distinct source. The limit lands on the client side: outbound connections draw source ports from the ephemeral range, 28,232 of them on default Linux, and that's per destination IP and port. Add TIME_WAIT holding each for 60 seconds and you cap around 470 new connections per second to a single upstream, no matter how much hardware you have.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

"A server can only handle 65,535 connections because there are only 65,535 ports." What's wrong with that?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know connections are identified by a tuple, not by a port.

It confuses the listening port with the connection identity. A server listens on one port — 443 — and every accepted connection shares it. What distinguishes them is the full four-tuple, and the client's IP and source port vary freely, so a single listening socket on port 443 can serve millions of simultaneous connections without any port pressure at all. The 65,535 limit applies to how many distinct services a host can listen on, which is a completely different question and one nobody actually hits.

The server's real ceiling is file descriptors and memory: one descriptor per connection against ulimit -n, plus send and receive buffers. That's why the first symptom of a connection-count problem on a server is EMFILE: too many open files — an error that looks like a filesystem problem and is actually the network limit wearing a disguise. Where the port ceiling does bite is the client side, and specifically a client talking to one upstream endpoint. There the destination IP and port are fixed, the source IP is fixed, and the only varying element is the source port — so you genuinely have just the ephemeral range to spend. This is the asymmetry worth stating out loud, because it's the part people get backwards.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

An API gateway proxying to one backend service starts throwing EADDRNOTAVAIL. What's happening and what do you change?

📍 Seen in the wild: the sidecar/gateway version of port exhaustion, which arrives looking like an upstream failure.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can do the arithmetic and then pick a fix that isn't a sysctl.

EADDRNOTAVAIL on connect() means the kernel could not find a free source port for the four-tuple — the gateway has exhausted the ephemeral range against that one backend. The arithmetic: 28,232 ports, each held 60 seconds after an active close by TIME_WAIT, gives roughly 470 new connections per second sustained. A gateway opening a fresh connection per request hits that at 470 rps, which is a trivially small number and always a shock to people who assumed the limit was somewhere near "thousands of connections".

The fixes, in the order they should be tried. Connection pooling with keep-alive is the real answer — at 470 rps with a 20ms backend, Little's Law puts concurrency near 10, so a pool of 50 connections serves the traffic and creates ~50 sockets total rather than 470 per second. Give the backend more addresses: the ceiling is per destination IP and port, so four backend IPs behind a DNS name quadruple it, which is one reason service discovery returning multiple A records is more useful than it looks. Widen the range with net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="10240 65535" for about 55,000 ports — worth doing, but it's a factor of two, not a fix. net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 lets the kernel reuse TIME_WAIT tuples for outbound connections when timestamps prove safety; it's legitimate and effective for a client. What you don't do is tcp_tw_recycle — removed from Linux in 4.12 because it broke clients behind NAT.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Limit Default Side it binds Symptom
ulimit -n (file descriptors) 1024 (often), 1M+ when raised Server, and any high-fan-out client EMFILE: too many open files
Ephemeral port range 32768–60999 = 28,232 Client, per destination IP:port EADDRNOTAVAIL on connect()
TIME_WAIT hold 60s (2×MSL) Active closer Divides the port range into a per-second rate
somaxconn (accept queue) 4096 on modern Linux Server Connection timeouts; accept-queue overflow counter
Socket buffer memory tcp_rmem/tcp_wmem Server at high connection count Memory pressure long after EMFILE
IANA dynamic range 49152–65535 Registry convention only Linux's default differs — don't quote the RFC as the Linux value

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The whole asymmetry is in that diagram. The server varies nothing — one IP, one port — and still gets unlimited tuples, because the client supplies the varying half. The client, talking to a fixed destination, has only its source port to vary, and so owns the scarce resource. Ports are per-protocol too: TCP 443 and UDP 443 are independent namespaces.

Sustained outbound connection rate to one endpoint = ephemeral_ports ÷ TIME_WAIT_seconds. Default Linux: 28,232 ÷ 60 ≈ **470 connections/sec**. Widened range (10240–65535): 55,295 ÷ 60 ≈ 920/sec. The multiplier that actually scales is distinct destination IP:port pairs — 4 backend IPs gives 4× — because each pair gets its own port space.

RFC 6056 is why ports are chosen randomly rather than sequentially: a predictable source port helps an off-path attacker forge segments into your connection. The cost is a small chance of collision with a TIME_WAIT tuple, which is what tcp_tw_reuse resolves using timestamps.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't raise ulimit -n to a million and consider the problem solved. Descriptors are free; the socket buffers behind them are not. At 100k connections with default tcp_rmem, you're committing gigabytes of kernel memory, and the failure moves from a clear EMFILE to an OOM kill that tells you nothing.

  • Don't widen the ephemeral range as your primary fix. It buys a factor of two on a limit that pooling removes entirely. Widening is headroom; pooling is the answer.

  • Don't assume the limit is per host. It's per (source IP, destination IP, destination port). One client hitting four backends has four separate port budgets — which is why the same code can be fine behind a DNS name returning several A records and fall over the moment someone puts a single VIP in front of them.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A server can't exceed 65,535 concurrent connections."

✅ Reality: Connections are identified by the four-tuple, so a single listening port serves millions. The server's limit is descriptors and memory. The port ceiling is a client-side limit, per destination endpoint.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I thought TIME_WAIT sockets were a memory problem to be minimised. They're cheap in memory — the cost is that each one holds a port out of a small range, which converts into a hard connections-per-second ceiling. Reframing it from "memory waste" to "rate limit" is what makes the 470/sec number obvious rather than surprising.

notes.title: When UDP Is Right

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
Give me the actual test for reaching for UDP.
Tier 2 — Trade-off
You've chosen UDP. What do you now owe, and where do teams get it wrong?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • UDP specification — RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol

  • DNS's transport rules — and when it falls back to TCP — RFC 1035 §4.2: Transport

  • Reliability rebuilt on UDP — RFC 9000: QUIC

  • What UDP omits, and what you must add back — High Performance Browser Networking: Building Blocks of UDP

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one-line test for choosing UDP? Is the data worthless by the time a retransmission would arrive?
Safe payload size before fragmentation? ~1472 bytes on 1500 MTU; 1232 is the safe modern figure.
What must you add back yourself? Congestion control, and usually keepalives for NAT mappings.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

UDP is right when a retransmission would arrive too late to be useful, or when the exchange is so short that a handshake would dominate it. Live audio, video frames, game state and sensor telemetry all fit the first case — the next update supersedes the lost one, so resending is worse than useless. DNS fits the second: a 60-byte query where 1 RTT of setup would double the cost. What you take on is everything TCP gave you free, and the one you cannot skip is congestion control — which is exactly why QUIC exists rather than everyone rolling their own.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Give me the actual test for reaching for UDP.

🎯 Really testing: whether you have a rule, or a list of examples you've memorised.

One question decides most cases: is this data still useful after one RTT of delay? If no, UDP — because TCP's only tool is retransmission, and retransmitting data that has expired costs you a stall and buys you nothing. A 20ms audio frame that arrives 200ms late is not late audio, it's noise; the jitter buffer conceals the gap and the listener hears nothing. If yes, you're on TCP unless something else is unusual.

Two secondary tests catch the rest. Would the handshake dominate? For a single short request/response — DNS, NTP, a discovery probe — 1 RTT of setup on top of 1 RTT of exchange doubles the cost, which is why those protocols are all UDP. And do you need one socket to serve unbounded peers, or multicast at all? TCP can do neither. Everything else is a TCP question. Note what is not on the list: throughput. UDP's 12-byte header saving is irrelevant at realistic payload sizes, and anyone justifying UDP on efficiency grounds will be asked to quantify it.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

You've chosen UDP. What do you now owe, and where do teams get it wrong?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up that separates people who've shipped a UDP protocol from people who've chosen one.

Four things, and they're rarely all remembered. Congestion control is the non-negotiable one: sending at volume with no backoff is antisocial, gets policed by intermediaries, and collapses rather than degrades under contention. Datagram sizing — stay under the path MTU (~1472 bytes on Ethernet, 1232 as the safe modern figure) or IP fragmentation reintroduces all-or-nothing loss at a worse granularity, since losing one fragment discards the whole datagram. Keepalives, because NAT gateways drop idle UDP mappings in as little as 30 seconds with no notification to either side, so any long-lived UDP flow needs its own heartbeat. And a TCP fallback, because enough corporate and mobile networks block UDP on non-53 ports that a client-facing UDP protocol without one simply doesn't work for some users.

Where teams get it wrong is the slope from there. Having added sequence numbers to detect loss, they add acknowledgements to report it, then retransmission, then a window — and have arrived at a worse TCP, in userspace, with none of the decades of tuning. The discipline is to notice the second step and stop: if you need ordering and reliability, you want QUIC, which is that work done properly with per-stream recovery and a real congestion controller. The legitimate UDP protocols are the ones that never add reliability at all — RTP concealing loss, StatsD dropping samples, DNS retrying the whole query — and it's worth being able to name that boundary, because "we built reliable UDP" is a claim a senior reviewer will probe hard.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Use case Why UDP wins What it adds back Fallback when UDP is blocked
DNS Handshake would double a sub-ms lookup Client-side retry; truncation bit Retries the query over TCP — built into the protocol
VoIP / video (RTP) Late audio is worthless; concealment beats retransmission Jitter buffer, FEC, loss concealment TURN relay over TCP, at a real quality cost
QUIC / HTTP/3 Per-stream loss recovery, no connection-wide stall Full reliability + congestion control in userspace HTTP/2 over TCP via Alt-Svc
Metrics / StatsD Never block the app; no per-agent collector state Nothing — loss is accepted by design Batched HTTP POST when correctness matters
Game state Latest state supersedes lost state Snapshot/delta encoding, client prediction Usually none; the game degrades
Service discovery / mDNS Multicast, which TCP cannot do Periodic re-announcement Unicast to a registry

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The sizing arithmetic is the part most often skipped, and it has a clean answer:

Max UDP payload before fragmentation = MTU − 20 (IPv4 header) − 8 (UDP header). On standard 1500-byte Ethernet: 1472 bytes. Inside a VPC with 9001-byte jumbo frames: 8973. Across a tunnel or VPN, lower — which is why 1232 bytes is the widely used safe figure (1280-byte IPv6 minimum MTU less 40 IPv6 and 8 UDP headers).

Why it matters: IP fragmentation splits one datagram across packets, and losing any fragment discards the entire datagram. Fragmenting a 4 KB datagram into three doesn't give you graceful degradation; it triples your effective loss rate.

DNS is the cleanest illustration of the whole note, because it contains its own exception: queries go over UDP for the handshake reason, and when a response won't fit the server sets the truncation bit and the resolver retries the identical query over TCP. One protocol, both transports, chosen per message shape rather than per application — which is the pattern the Tier 1 test is really pointing at.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not when you're about to add reliability on top. The moment you write sequence numbers and retransmission, you are building TCP with fewer engineer-decades behind it. Use QUIC. This is the single most common way a UDP decision goes wrong, and it degrades slowly enough that nobody notices until the protocol is load-bearing.

  • Not for client-facing traffic without a TCP fallback. UDP on non-53 ports is blocked often enough that a meaningful slice of users simply won't connect, and they won't be able to tell you why. Worse, the fallback can silently carry most of your traffic — monitor the ratio, or you'll have paid for a benefit you never received.

  • Not when a batched HTTP POST would do. The honest cheaper alternative for most telemetry: at thousands of events per second rather than hundreds of thousands, HTTP gives you retries, auth, TLS, proxy compatibility and observability for free, and the UDP path buys nothing you can measure.

  • Not without your own loss counters. UDP loss is invisible on both sides. netstat -su receive-buffer errors and your own sequence-gap counters are the only evidence you'll ever get, and if you didn't build them you will diagnose the incident from a dashboard gap.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "UDP is the choice when you need speed."

✅ Reality: It's the choice when late data is worthless, or when the handshake dominates a short exchange. On an uncongested path both protocols move data at line rate. Framing it as speed leads to UDP being chosen for bulk transfer, where it's simply worse.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I read QUIC as evidence that UDP is the modern default and TCP is legacy. QUIC isn't an endorsement of UDP's semantics — it treats UDP as a substrate, a way to get packets past middleboxes while implementing reliability, ordering and congestion control itself. The lesson is the opposite of "prefer UDP": it's that these guarantees are so necessary that a new protocol rebuilt every one of them rather than doing without.
